content.title: About
content.content: Lambsquarter (Chenopodium album), also known as goosefoot, is an annual herb widely distributed in temperate regions. When cooked, its leaves become tender with a mild nutty flavor and a hint of sweetness. Cooked lambsquarter is commonly used in soups, stews, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lambsquarter has been consumed since ancient Greek and Roman times.
Its seeds are ground into a protein‑rich flour used for baking.
The plant grows quickly and is often called a "nutritional weed" because it can be harvested from the wild.
Leaves are high in vitamins A and C, as well as iron and calcium.
In some cultures the leaves are boiled with milk to make a nourishing drink.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A and C
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision and immunity, while vitamin C acts as an antioxidant protecting cells.

items.title: Source of iron and calcium
items.content: These minerals are essential for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: Protein from lambsquarter helps meet daily amino‑acid needs, especially in vegetarian diets.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Cooked lambsquarter is virtually fat‑free, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber content promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: High oxalate levels may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people may be allergic to plants in the amaranth family.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Raw leaves contain oxalic acid and should always be cooked before consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked lambsquarter can be served as a side dish, added to vegetable soups, stews, or salads. It is also used as a filling for pies and pancakes. Before cooking, rinse the leaves well and trim any tough stems.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked lambsquarter in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze portions in freezer bags at –18 °C, where they retain quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Seafood salad is a cold dish made from a mixture of cooked or poached seafood (shrimp, mussels, squid, crab meat) combined with vegetables, herbs, and a light dressing based on mayonnaise, yogurt or olive oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Seafood salad is a staple in Mediterranean and Asian cuisines.
There are many variations, including avocado, mango, rice or noodle additions.
Seafood is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, which are heart‑healthy.
The salad is often served as an appetizer at festive gatherings and seafood restaurants.
Lemon or lime juice is commonly added for a bright, tangy flavor.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Seafood provides EPA and DHA, fatty acids that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: The salad supplies all essential amino acids, aiding muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: It contains zinc, iron, iodine, vitamin B12 and vitamin D, important for immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Low calorie with light dressing
items.content: Using a yogurt‑based or olive‑oil dressing keeps the dish light yet satisfying.

items.title: Supports brain function
items.content: Omega‑3 and vitamin B12 contribute to improved cognition and mood.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels, or other shellfish.

items.title: Food poisoning risk
items.content: Improperly handled seafood can harbor bacteria and toxins; ensure thorough cooking and proper storage.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared dressings and canned seafood often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Certain seafood (e.g., crab meat) contains cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as an appetizer or light main. Pair it with whole‑grain bread, crackers, or use it as a filling for wraps. For a lighter option, swap mayonnaise for a yogurt‑herb dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, store seafood and vegetables separately and combine just before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato is a tuberous root belonging to the Convolvulaceae family. It has a naturally sweet flavor, orange‑red flesh, and is rich in nutrients. It is commonly prepared as a casserole, mashed side dish, or baked wedges.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potato is not a true potato; it belongs to a different botanical family.
There are over 400 varieties, with flesh colors ranging from orange and yellow to white and purple.
It was domesticated in Central and South America more than 5,000 years ago.
In Japan, sweet potato is often served as a sweet casserole called "daifuku".
Sweet potatoes contain more beta‑carotene than regular potatoes.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: The orange flesh provides provitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Carbohydrates are released slowly, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6, important for protein metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides potassium, magnesium, and iron, which are essential for heart and muscle function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to sweet potato.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: High intake may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible persons.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Because of its natural sweetness, people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweet potatoes can be baked, steamed, boiled and mashed, or used in casseroles. Peel before cooking, though the skin is edible and fiber‑rich. Pair with spices such as cinnamon, nutmeg, or rosemary for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sweet potatoes in a cool, dark, dry place at 55‑60 °F (13‑16 °C). Do not refrigerate, as cold temperatures can alter texture and flavor. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator wrapped in a paper bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Tortilla is a thin, flat roundbread made from corn or wheat flour, traditionally used in Mexican cuisine. The NFS (2584) version is a ready‑to‑eat tortilla produced with a gluten‑free process, high in fiber and with a low glycemic index.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Originally tortillas were made from masa (ground corn), but modern versions often use wheat flour.
A traditional Mexican tortilla is about 15 cm in diameter and 1–2 mm thick.
Tortillas serve as the base for tacos, burritos, quesadillas and chips.
In the United States more than 3 billion tortillas are consumed each year.
The NFS technology preserves the natural grain flavor while reducing gluten content.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: NFS tortilla contains both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: A low GI makes the tortilla suitable for people monitoring glucose levels and helps sustain satiety.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide a steady energy release without sharp insulin spikes.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The product is fortified with thiamine, niacin and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many baked goods, NFS tortilla has minimal fat, making it a light snack option.

items.title: Corn or wheat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to the ingredients.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain varieties contain added salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten in wheat version
items.content: If you are gluten‑sensitive, choose the corn (gluten‑free) version.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the tortilla on a dry skillet, in the microwave, or in the oven, then use it as a base for tacos, burritos, wraps, chips, or simply enjoy it with dips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep tortillas in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. After opening, store in the refrigerator for up to 7 days or freeze for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: A vegetable sandwich on white bread consists of fresh vegetables (tomato, cucumber, lettuce, pepper), a slice of cheese and a light sauce, placed between two soft white bread slices. It is suitable for a light snack or a quick lunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White bread provides a soft, neutral base that lets the bright flavors of the vegetables shine.
Vegetables are often served raw in the sandwich, preserving maximum vitamins and a crunchy texture.
This sandwich is popular in vegetarian and vegan diets when the cheese is replaced with a plant‑based alternative.
It is easily adaptable – avocado, hummus or pickled veggies can be added for extra flavor.
White‑bread sandwiches are commonly served in school cafeterias and fast‑food cafés.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Fresh vegetables supply vitamins A, C, K and folate.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Vegetables and any added seeds boost dietary fiber, supporting digestion.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: A white‑bread sandwich is generally modest in calories, making it a good option for weight management.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High‑water vegetables like cucumber and tomato help maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Compounds such as lycopene and carotenoids in the veggies act as antioxidants.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to cheese, seeds (e.g., sesame) or sauces.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces or salty cheese can raise the sodium level.

items.title: Hygiene
items.content: Fresh vegetables should be thoroughly washed to avoid food‑borne illness.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: White bread contains gluten, so the sandwich is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat the sandwich right after assembling, cutting it in half if desired. It is convenient to take it on the go in a wrapper or parchment paper. Optional additions include mustard, hummus or a light yogurt sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator in an airtight container for no more than 24 hours. The bread may become soft, so it is best to assemble the sandwich shortly before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetarian, fillet is a plant‑based substitute for meat fillet made from soy protein, wheat gluten and vegetable oils. It has a mild, chicken‑like flavor and a firm, juicy texture. It is used in dishes where quick cooking and a light meat replacement are desired.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product is completely vegetarian and contains no animal ingredients.
Soy protein provides a high amount of plant‑based protein.
Natural flavorings are often added to mimic the taste of chicken.
Vegetarian, fillet can be grilled, baked, pan‑fried or microwaved.
It typically has lower saturated fat than traditional meat fillet.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: One piece supplies about 15 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low cholesterol
items.content: Unlike meat, the product contains no cholesterol, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Added wheat gluten and vegetable fibers help normal digestion.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Soy protein is rich in vitamin B12 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: When not seasoned, it fits well into low‑salt diets.

items.title: Soy or gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains soy protein and wheat gluten, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Added fats
items.content: Some versions include vegetable oils, so total calorie intake should be considered.

items.title: Thermal processing
items.content: Insufficient cooking may leave a faint "meaty" odor that some people find off‑putting.

items.title: Sodium in ready‑to‑eat versions
items.content: Pre‑seasoned fillet can be high in salt; check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The fillet can be pan‑fried, baked, steamed or added to salads and sandwiches. Before cooking, rinse the pieces in cold water and pat dry. It pairs well with soy sauce, spices, lemon juice and fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C. Once opened, use within 5‑7 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for up to 3 months. Do not store above 10 °C to prevent spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Veggie burger is a plant‑based patty made from a blend of vegetables, legumes and whole grains, shaped into a burger and served on a soft bun. It offers a tasty alternative to traditional meat burgers, suitable for vegetarians and anyone looking to reduce meat consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The patty provides over 30% of its calories from plant protein, mainly pea and soy isolates.
Common ingredients include carrot, beetroot and spinach, giving the burger a vibrant color and extra vitamins.
Oats or quinoa are often added to improve texture and moisture retention.
A gluten‑free version is possible by using a gluten‑free bun and grain‑free binders.
Many recipes are fortified with B‑vitamins and iron to match the nutritional profile of meat.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Pea and soy protein support muscle growth and repair, providing a complete amino acid profile.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, the burger contains mostly poly‑ and monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Vegetables and whole grains add dietary fiber, aiding digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The burger supplies vitamin A, vitamin C, iron and potassium, important for immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Environmental benefits
items.content: Plant‑based burgers require less water and land than beef, resulting in a lower carbon footprint.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Soy protein is a common allergen; individuals with soy sensitivity should avoid this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: To enhance flavor, the burger may contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Gluten (if regular bun is used)
items.content: A standard wheat bun introduces gluten, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Processed ingredients
items.content: Some versions include preservatives and flavor enhancers; choose minimally processed options when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the veggie burger on a warmed bun with lettuce, tomato, onion, mustard or ketchup. For extra crunch, grill or pan‑sear the patty before assembling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the fresh burger refrigerated at 0–4 °C for up to 3 days. Frozen versions store for up to 3 months; thaw in the refrigerator before cooking.

wheat-bread-as-ingredient-in-sandwiches.title: Wheat Bread as Ingredient in Sandwiches

content.title: About
content.content: Wheat bread is a baked product made from wheat flour, water, yeast, and salt. It has a soft crumb, light crust, and neutral flavor, making it an ideal base for sandwiches. The bread acts as a “container” for fillings, allowing a wide variety of ingredients to be combined.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat bread is one of the most widely consumed breads worldwide.
Traditional recipes rely on fermentation, which enhances flavor and digestibility.
Different cultures have their own versions, from French baguette to American white sandwich loaf.
Stale bread can be toasted into croutons for extra crunch.
Many varieties include seeds, nuts, or whole grains for added texture and nutrition.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat bread provides a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, which support metabolism and the nervous system.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions are rich in fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Bread contains iron, magnesium, and zinc, important for blood formation and immunity.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of carbs and a modest amount of protein helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Gluten intolerance
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White wheat bread can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes, which may be undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some breads are high in sodium; those monitoring salt intake should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Commercial loaves may contain emulsifiers, dough conditioners, and other additives that some individuals prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use wheat bread as the base for sandwiches, spread sauces, and add lettuce, vegetables, meats, fish, or cheese. It can be lightly toasted for a crunchy crust or kept soft for cold fillings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag – it stays fresh for up to 2 months. Thaw before use and toast if desired.

content.title: About
content.content: Worcestershire sauce is a fermented condiment made from vinegar, molasses, anchovies, tamarind, onion, garlic, and a blend of spices. It was created in England in the early 19th century and is now widely used to flavor meats, soups, cocktails, and marinades.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recipe was developed in 1823 in the town of Worcester, giving the sauce its name.
Traditional fermentation takes several months, during which the sauce matures in oak barrels.
Worcestershire sauce is often called the “secret ingredient” in the Bloody Mary cocktail recipe.
The original formula includes anchovies, but vegetarian versions without fish are also available.
In the US the sauce is commonly used in “Corned Beef”, while in the UK it appears in “Steak and sauce” dishes.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Contains polyphenols from tamarind and vinegar that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Vinegar and enzymes aid in the breakdown of food.

items.title: Provides trace minerals
items.content: The sauce supplies iron, calcium, and magnesium from anchovies and spices.

items.title: Low‑calorie flavor enhancer
items.content: Small amounts add taste without significantly increasing a dish’s calorie count.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: Fermentation creates beneficial bacteria that may support gut microbiota.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Traditional sauce contains anchovies, which can trigger reactions in people allergic to fish.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salt is used generously, so individuals with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Molasses and other sweeteners add a modest amount of sugar, which may be a concern for diabetics.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Vinegar makes the sauce acidic; excessive consumption may irritate the stomach.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add Worcestershire sauce to marinades, barbecue sauces, soups, stews, and cocktails such as Bloody Mary. A teaspoon is usually enough to impart a deep, savory flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in a tightly sealed bottle in the refrigerator after opening. When stored properly it retains its flavor for up to 12 months. Discard if you notice off‑odors or mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit-flavored whole‑milk yogurt is a fermented dairy product made by culturing whole milk with live Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus cultures, then adding fruit puree or juice for flavor. It has a creamy texture, mild dairy taste, and a bright fruit note.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yogurt has been known since ancient Mesopotamia, where it was used to preserve milk.
Fruit yogurts appeared in the early 20th century when manufacturers began adding fruit purees to improve taste.
Live cultures in yogurt help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.
Whole‑milk yogurt contains more fat and vitamins A and D than low‑fat versions.
In many cultures yogurt is traditionally served with honey and nuts.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Probiotic cultures promote a balanced intestinal flora, aiding digestion and nutrient absorption.

items.title: Source of calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Whole milk provides high levels of calcium and vitamin D, essential for bone health.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Yogurt supplies complete protein important for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains notable amounts of B2 and B12, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from fruit
items.content: Fruit puree adds antioxidants such as vitamin C and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming whole‑milk yogurt.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein or whey can occur in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Fruit yogurts often contain added sugars; choose low‑sugar options when possible.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Whole‑milk yogurt is more calorie‑dense than low‑fat versions, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy it as a snack, blend into smoothies, top oatmeal or granola, or use as a base for sauces and desserts. Garnish with fresh berries or nuts for extra texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store yogurt in the refrigerator at 2–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
